utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Closed session to allow the witness to come into court, please. Can we have the blinds down at the security end, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, K79.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Marcussen will now continue. Please bear in mind that the oath, the declaration you took at the beginning to tell the truth continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, K79.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to start out by refreshing the witness's member on some point based on his statement, about some evidence where we left off yesterday. There was a legal issue that arose yesterday as to whether or not we can do that, and there is a decision by the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic case, decision on interlocutory appeal relating to the refreshment of the memory of a witness. The case number is IT-01-47-AR79.2 [sic], and it is of 2nd April, 2004. I have prepared a bundle of material with some decision and some other jurisprudence to hand around if necessary. There is reference in that decision to another Appeals Chamber decision in the Blagoje Simic case, that is a decision of the 23rd of May. That is also included in the bundle, and there are guidelines issued by at least two Trial Chambers where refreshment memory based on a prior statement has been allowed. So I propose if the court officer would hand around that material then Your Honours and the Defence can have a look at that if there's an issue. But otherwise, if I may, I will proceed with the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there anything else you want to draw our attention to on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I had a look at this yesterday and it's pretty plain this course of action is permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I went through the documents this morning so we withdraw the objection from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have very much in mind we have a ruling to make on your objections on the admissibility of the evidence in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We got past that stage yesterday, Mr. Marcussen. He accepted he had given a statement and that it was signed by him. We're now at the question of clarifying the particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Also, just before we get to that, when you came to The Hague in preparation of your testimony, did you have a chance to look at that statement again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you make some -- did you make some -- did you note some mistakes in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could we give a B/C/S copy -- a B/C/S copy of the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is now in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm informed that it is uploaded as a Defence exhibit, and I think we also have given it an exhibit number yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have a number, and let's have it on the screen, please. This should be prepared for today. We've got time constraints and everything should be thoroughly well organised so we can make rapid progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: All I want to ask here is the witness whether you could look at the statement and whether the corrections you made were to paragraph 29 and paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Exhibit number is 6D180, Your Honours. While the witness is looking at the statement, just to be sure we -- we cover this later on, I would like the Defence Exhibit 6D180 be placed under seal as well as the other exhibits we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, I think if you look at -- if I may help you, the last sentence of paragraph 29. Did you make a correction to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then if you could go to the -- to paragraph 39, towards the end of paragraph 39?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, my learned friend is referring to the number of an exhibit tendered by the Defence, but as I heard yesterday, and I hope I noted it down correctly, the statement bears number P2653. This was the number given by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But he has chosen to use 6D180, and there's nothing to stop him had doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And it's only that the Prosecution exhibit, as I understand, is not uploaded into the system, so we couldn't call it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we see no problem with him using a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, am I correct you also made a correction to paragraph 39?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But when you reviewed the statement prior to testifying, they were the only two errors you saw in the statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This doesn't sound to me like refreshing memory. This sounds to me like challenging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My next question is this: If I were to show another paragraph -- if I were to show some other parts of your statement to you, do you think that would help you recollect some of the other events in the statement that you testified about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you then to take a look at paragraphs 34 and 35, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In -- in the last part of paragraph 34 the statement says that your platoon commander, "... told us that the company commander had ordered that we were to search all houses in the village of Ljubizda and any Albanians who were still there had to be deported. That was when the looting really started." Is that -- does that refresh your memory about the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is this a correct description now that you have seen this? Is this how you would describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be expelled, not deported - that may be an error - to the road leading from Suva Reka to Prizren, that they should be expelled from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the next paragraph, paragraph 35, you say that: "In Ljubizda, we went from house to house forcing out the occupants and ordering them to leave Kosovo. I didn't see anyone killed, but there was mistreatment and people were beaten up. Two or three houses were burned and the company stole the people's belongings." Now, having looked at the statement, do you think this is a correct description? Does that sound like what you remember the events to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not all the policemen. Two or three policemen did that. I'm referring to the looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But -- but otherwise it's -- it's a correct description that the occupants were forced out? There was some mistreatment, although nobody were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If he's going to change what the meaning of what the statement is, then the question is meaningless. If he's going to cite exactly the what the statement says and put it to the witness, then that's the only way he can do. I don't agree with this tactic of all of a sudden changing what is said and then giving it to the witness and asking him if that's correct, isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness said that the statement was a correct reflection and then he made a modification and said it was only two or three policemen, and I wanted to make sure that the modification he's making is only in relation to how many people were involved in the looting and the clarification on that point. He had -- I had already read out the paragraph. He said this is a correct reflection; then he had a modification to part of it and all I'm doing is trying to find out the scope of that modification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the way to do that is to confirm whether he maintains that people were beaten up, which is the point you're trying to clarify. Don't paraphrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, so is it correct that your company went from house to house and forced occupants out of the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were they ordered to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To leave their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this was asked and answered previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But now we're refreshing the witness memory and the statement to specifically deal with this issue, and we're trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't have it both ways, Mr. Lukic. If Mr. Ivetic insists on the statement being scrupulously adhered to, then Mr. Marcussen is entitled to go back over it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So on this point, there's an error in the statement? Is that right, K79? This is not a correct reflection of how you remember it today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you didn't see anybody get killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were -- were some people beaten and mistreated though?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three Albanians perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and were -- were two or three houses burned down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think two houses were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could interrupt you briefly there. You were making efforts, yesterday, to try to secure more sitting time today, and a great deal of effort's been put into that with a view to trying to complete the evidence of the witness, and it is possible for us to sit to 3.30 today if that's going to achieve the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Having reviewed my own notes and having discussed with my learned friends on the other side who have been very accommodating, I -- I do not think that we will be able to -- to achieve the objective of finishing the witness even if we sit all this time. I think in light of some of the issues that have come up, we must have some cross-examination and I will have to probably spend little more time than I optimistically hoped yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When do you expect to finish this examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, we have been keeping good progress so if we could keep this speed, then I may be done may be in half an hour or a little less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will allow more than four hours to the Defence for cross-examination. Would that be sufficient? It would be roughly equivalent to the examination-in-chief, so there is a possibility and I think we should go for it, if we can. If we fail we fail, but we should try. If we are going to do that, then we'll sit according to the lengthier day schedule, which means that this session would go to 10.45, and then we will follow the time we would normally follow if we were sitting until 3.30. So let's proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I see that I will probably need some time for re-examination, so that's also one of the reasons why I am -- we're all happy to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, I'll now sort of proceed with the chronology of events from where we stopped yesterday, and we talked a little bit about you seeing refugees on -- on the road between Suva Reka and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I should maybe ask if the usher could retrieve the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, K79. You were to see the statement for some specific purposes. We'll withdraw that. K79, how long did you stay in Korisa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our base was there for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And while you were there did you see anybody get killed by members of your detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same objection as yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. That's noted, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain for us what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A policeman killed a farmer, an elderly Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before killing the elderly Albanian, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He took ten German marks from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who killed this elderly Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session, then we can develop this a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did your company commander know about this, do you think? Sorry, let me rephrase that. Did your company commander know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think he knew. I'm not sure, but I don't think he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where were you -- do you remember where you were on the 20th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the 20th of April, we were doing the village of Budakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you say "we were doing the village," what do you mean by doing the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mopping it up of KLA members. That's the term we used for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And during this operation, did you witness anybody being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same objection as before, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's noted, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, would you -- would you tell us what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two young men were killed on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you see him kill -- kill these two men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I and three or four other policemen saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you tell us what these -- the men that were killed looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were about 30, approximately 30 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were they wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you saw them did they have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would ask that we go into -- if we could go into private session. I would like to cover the incident where we started on some photographs yesterday. So if we can, first of all, go in and continue with that incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My apologies. We have had heard evidence from Witness Latifi about this area about events that were earlier, but about a campaign that started on the 25th, 26th of February. So this is obviously taking time -- taking place after that event. So I just wanted to make that clear. Our arguments as to why this is relevant are the same. I'm not going to open that all up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, did you participate in an operation in Bukos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's noted that Mr. Lukic objects again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where is Bukos? Is there a bigger down that's close to it that you know the name of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the direction of Budakovo. From Suva Reka, it's a small village there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Approximately, how far from Suva Reka, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About ten kilometres or so, more or less. I don't know exactly, but I think that would be the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During this operation, did you see anybody getting killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you -- could you describe for us what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four KLA members were captured, put in a house, and a grenade was thrown in through a window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did -- did you see the men being put into the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you see the grenade -- how many grenades were thrown in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was some 20 metres from where we stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And who -- who threw in the grenade -- or grenades, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People from the 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have been taking this sort of -- redacting this sort of information. I think we should take the reference to the 2nd Company out from the public version and redact it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have -- we have kept the detachment numbers and all these other things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you don't know the detachment number. You don't know the unit number. I mean, it could be the 2nd Company of any detachment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was from our detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. On this operation, were there anybody else with you other than the -- the PJP that were with you during this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were the people from the Suva Reka utility company. They had a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what was their function during the operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They collected the bodies of the dead KLA members after the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know what they did with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, I'd like now to go back to -- to 1998. Well, I guess maybe even before with a general question. Do you know of a unit called the -- referred to as the JSO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the unit for special operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how was this unit armed compared to your -- the things, the equipment that you had in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had better weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you know the unit before you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What kind of a reputation did the JSO had among you -- you policemen in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Its reputation was as a good and capable unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that unit was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ulemek, nicknamed "Legija," was the commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everybody knew that, and I, in fact, saw him once in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that in just a little bit; but before I do that, did -- do you know who his superior was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Frenki up until July, August 1998, and after that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know what Frenki's family name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him in Srbica in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When in 1998 did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was that in connection with an operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them after an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you ever participate in an operation where the JSO also participated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If we were unable to take a place, they would come in and finish the job. So we never actually were in action together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you ever in areas where they had first been in action and then the PJP was deployed afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in Donja Lausa [Realtime transcript read in error "Gornja Lausa"] and Gornja Lausa near Srbica, and also at Budakovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's also noted, Mr. Lukic. I think actually the two names, which are identical in the transcript, were actually different in what the witness said. I think he may have said "Donja Lausa and Gornja Lausa," but perhaps that came be -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe the operation in 1998? Did the JSO do anything in particular that you remember during the operation we talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a very big stronghold of the KLA, Gornja Lausa and Donja Lausa, and they cleaned up this area of KLA members. But we got there afterwards, so we didn't see them in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you -- had anything happened to -- to the houses in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The houses were burnt down, but I don't know who set them on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you involved in an operation that started at Drenica and went through Glogovac and towards Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the JSO --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Noted, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we have evidence from Kadriu and maybe Gerxhaliu about some of this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it's outside the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, did -- did the JSO participate in this operation that I just mentioned last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: During the different -- I'm moving to something else now. During the operations that you participated in, was there, from what you saw, any VJ infantrymen with you at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any members of the army steal or loot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain -- well, let's -- let's cover this. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near Korisa, on the road. This man was robbing the refugees, and he got arrested by two captains that were -- happened to be close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before -- before getting arrested, who did he ask money from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Albanians in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No one else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a military vehicle in the column and he asked this army captain for some money, and that's when they actually arrested him. He was drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever -- you have mentioned a number of crimes that have been committed -- that were committed by different members of the MUP. Did you ever see any of them get arrested while you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Two members of my detachment were arrested. It was near Vranje, on their way back to their weakened leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in their car they had some VCRs, cameras, TV sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who arrested them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police from Vranje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did anybody of the specific people -- the people that -- that committed the crimes that we have been talking about yesterday and today, did they ever get arrested?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when he was arrested? K79, do you know when -- well, yes. We need a redaction then of the name at page 29, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, we have that, Mr. Marcussen. Question is do you know when the commander was arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime in August or September last year. I'm not sure, but I think that was the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- when did you leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you continue to work as a policeman after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What about the other members of your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you at some point start to speak openly about the crimes you have -- that you had seen in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen, does this need to be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We should. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think from the -- from line 12 of paragraph 24 to line -- so page 25, line 4 should be redacted, and we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will reverse the order of the indictment and begin with General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness K79.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic. Before me I have your statement which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, and the testimony you gave to this Court yesterday and today. We will have to go through your statement in detail because of some things that were said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there copies available in English, which would make it easier for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We can do that, but it's sometimes easier to have it available in hard copy when it's a contentious issue like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we -- my case manager foresaw that, and we have some -- I think it should go probably just to the Bench, the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we proceed to the statement you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal, I wish to put some general questions to you. You were in Kosovo as only part of one unit, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're going to be identifying --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- people and units. Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we are no longer in private session, I will skip over a part I was going to ask about and come back to it later. I will now ask you something about the statement you made to the Office of the Prosecutor. We don't see here where you made this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you recall, who was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Philip Caine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let's move to the statement. Is it correct that every member of the PJP individually received a brochure about the behaviour of policemen in times of war and adhering to wartime conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We didn't get it. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, when you speak of regular police duties, you said that you did normal police duties although you were a member of the PJP and that you were only called upon to attend, for example, demonstrations in Pristina or Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1st of September, 1998. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please redact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, redact that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever sent as a member of the PJP to a demonstration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought that the reserve detachment you mentioned was a reserve detachment of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And prior to the 1st of September, you were a member of that reserve detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that not mean that you were a member of the PJP before the 1st of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a manner of speaking, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I need to go to the private session. I think that we'll have to jump in and out very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you, yesterday, Exhibit P1600. These are camouflage uniforms worn by the PJP. You told us, yesterday, that those were NATO uniforms. Can we in fact agree that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I didn't show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I did not show P1600 to the witness. I think it was a witness earlier this week. It has been hectic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please -- in fact, we could look at this photograph, but I have a very brief question for you. Can we then agree that the green camouflage uniforms worn by the PJP were in fact made in Yugoslavia, but they were a copy of uniforms worn by the -- by NATO in their pattern. So those were not in effect the uniforms produced by NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were made in our country, but we called them NATO uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you used this term because of the pattern on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now something in relation to paragraph 10. Here you say that in the company that bore the same name as your detachment, and now don't let us mention the actual name, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, I actually saw them on only one occasion. They wore all kinds of uniforms. Some wore NATO uniforms. Some were blue uniforms. They only joined us when it was necessary in our detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we, in fact, agree on the following: You don't know whether they were in fact members of the company that has the same name as your detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were at Budakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Geographically speaking, they were in the same location as you were, but you don't know whether they were officially members of this company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were officially members, but they were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you something in relation to paragraphs 12 and 13 of your statement. You have a statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we can assist with a B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So paragraphs 12 and 13, but you don't have to read it yet. Let me ask you something related to what you said yesterday in your evidence. You speak about your arrival in Orahovac. At 9591, line 19, you say the following when asked by my learned colleague Mr. Marcussen, and again I will be reading in English so that we all get the correct interpretation: "[In English] How far did you go in the trucks, until where? "Answer: To Bela Crkva and then to the entrance into Orahovac. "Question: Did you get off the trucks there? "Answer: No. "Question: Can you describe what happened when you arrived at the entrance to Orahovac? "Answer: Fighting was still going on in town. "Question: And what did you -- what did you do? "Answer: We were waiting in the trucks. "Question: Did you come under fire? "Answer: No, not at that moment. "Question: Did you approach Orahovac further? "Answer: Yes. We went through all of Orahovac and went to the Serb neighbourhood up there." [Interpretation] Were the engines of the trucks idling all this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not when we stopped at the entrance into Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But when you moved through Orahovac, the engines were on all the time; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were those trucks covered by canvas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you pass through Orahovac on those trucks without stopping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You described to us yesterday how members of the SAJ captured an Albanian, beat him up, and how one of SAJ members killed him, shot him to death. So we can agree that in fact you saw all that from a moving truck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was not moving. We were at the entrance to the village, and there we were stationary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this did not happen at the hotel but at the entrance to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the gas station, the hotel, at the entrance, that's where we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was there with you when you saw this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were the policemen from my platoon and my squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we go into private session, could you give us the full names of the people who were with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can we go to the private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this: Do you know the full name and the duty of the -- in the unit of the person who actually fired the shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What weapon did he fire the shots from? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether any of the SAJ commanders were present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this in light of some other evidence: You said that you came to location Vran-stena, that you were under fire. This is in paragraphs 14 and 15 of your statement. In the three days that you spent there, did you kill any KLA members in light of the fact that you were under fire all this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found four KLA members there, and they were dead. They had been killed in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do with their bodies? Can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were buried there, I think. I think that they were buried right there in the trench where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we will not jeopardise disclosing your identity if you told us what company or what unit - just give us the designation number - that replaced you when you left that position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the 20th. It was a unit from Pirot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to move on to paragraph 19 and 20, and we will have to spend some time dealing with them. In paragraph 19 you say: "In one of these hamlets, five civilians were killed; two women were raped and then killed there; three men and two women were killed in one house; and in another one, an old woman and her son who was mentally ill." Were those two houses close to each other and were those murders committed at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was not at the same time, and those two houses were not close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you talk about these events, could you please tell us whether the reconnaissance squad was present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this first house where according to you three men and two women were killed, was any fire opened from that house on your unit as you approach the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But we did find a vest in there, a combat vest, and a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We got that from your evidence yesterday. Witness K78 gave evidence, gave a statement to the Prosecution; and in paragraph 13 of his statement, he states that fire was opened on you as you approached the houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify something. The reconnaissance squad was the first to approach the house. It's possible that they came under fire. But when we approach the house, there was no fire coming out of it. So this is something that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the same witness, K78, claims that his unit took a boy with them. He was one of those three men, and that he later escaped. So what he's saying is that it is not true that that three men were killed but only two. Would you agree with this or would you maintain what you said previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that so I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible at all, in light of the fact that you say that all three men were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that three men were killed, and I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. In paragraph 20, you claim the following: "I saw clearly

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have to redact and go to the private session. I'm sorry. I mentioned the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll redact line 3 of page 42, and we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my testimony be completed today? I have to travel home tomorrow. I have business I cannot postpone. I told the Office of the Prosecutor before I arrived here that I couldn't stay for longer than ten days. They said it would all be over in four or five days. I have to be home on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're doing our best to complete your testimony today. Whether we will or not will depend on how quickly we proceed. So let's get on -- under way again. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just need one brief clarification from Your Honours. Would I be allowed to refresh the witness's recollection regarding the Belgrade testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Have you loaded this into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I haven't. I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can be done if due course, but -- or can it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, it can't be done. It's just this issue of the Prosecution not being notified of the use of documents before cross-examination and the compliance with the Chamber's direction in that regard that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But where the issue is -- is challenging the witness's evidence on the basis of a prior statement, that's not necessarily a foreseeable course of action. And, therefore, we will allow the use of this statement, and it can be loaded into the system thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we received your statement from the Office of the Prosecutor, the one you gave in Belgrade; and on page 3 of that statement K052, 5862, the last paragraph speaking about the incident we discussed before, you say the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the private session, Your Honour? There are names mentioned in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to me it would be best to stay in private session until we complete this evidence, Mr. Lukic. It's becoming rather unsatisfactory, particularly when so many redactions have had to be made. So until we get to a stage where it's clear that you're not going to have to do this, we should stay in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not have anything whatsoever to do with the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the fighting in Orahovac, you said that you saw outside Orahovac members of the army of Yugoslavia, of the VJ. My question is this: Do you know for a fact that in the sector where you saw members of the VJ immediately before your arrival, there had been an attack on an army vehicle and on that occasion an officer was killed, two soldiers were wounded, and the rest of the soldiers who were there were kept prisoner by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry. I have problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are probably aware of the fact that the unit that you found there was sent to help the prisoners of the KLA and of saving the body of the fallen officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those were very strong positions [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was the only position where you actually saw any members of the VJ or a unit of the VJ in that moment in the Orahovica sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, if you allow me. We have problems in the transcript. Page 70, line 19, I think that the witness said, "Those were very strong positions of the KLA." We miss that part of -- of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm happy to accept that, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. K79, my colleague Lukic asked you and you confirmed that you knew about some arrested people and criminal charges that were issued. My question is: Do you know that a number of persons in the course of the stay of the so-called KLA in Orahovac were kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some 50 or so Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Again, problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know that the KLA entered Orahovac, five civilians were killed, two Serb women were raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware of the civilians. I don't know anything about the Serb women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a certain number of bodies that had been kidnapped in Orahovac were later on found in the Volujak cave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And they were buried in 2005 in the vicinity of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that they were buried, but I know that they had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. K79, in paragraph 36 of your statement, you say that the army behaved differently, that members of the army would be arrested if they were found looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also illustrated that by an example today. Can we then conclude that the VJ and its members acted professionally in every aspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my territory, yes. I don't know about the things elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. K79. I don't have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is all I had to ask this witness. Once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Looks like things have been going much more smoothly than expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: K79, just on the last point about the VJ, you were asked about your -- your statement and about the behaviour of -- of the VJ. Am I correct that when you talk about your knowledge of whether member of the VJ would get arrested if they committed a crime is based on that one time when you saw a member of the VJ getting arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I also heard other people talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were billeted in the military barracks in a MUP, in a special MUP installation as it was called. Could you explain to us, as you were entering the barracks, how would you get to those installations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would have to past through the barracks. There was a facility there that was used only by the MUP members who did not hail from Prizren. When we arrived there, this is where they were billeted, in those rooms. This is a special building within the barracks that was used exclusively by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you -- the entrance to the barracks, would there be some sort of a check-point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were soldiers and there was also a member of the police, and that was at the main gate where they could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was it your impression that it was a permanent installation, MUP installation, within the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It had been built before for those MUP members who did not hail from the area and had to be accommodated somewhere, and I'm talking about Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was it -- was it different in the first barracks where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're referring to Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You have been giving evidence about a number of crimes. Are they all crimes you yourself have witnessed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a helpful question. We've been into the detail with respect to each, and we have all the information the witness has to say about each of these events. This all-encompassing question doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The question which I wanted to get to which I hope is appropriate is:

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you hear of other crimes being committed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. That is beyond the scope of the cross. He should have asked it in direct if he had any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Surely that's correct, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm asking because in cross-examination, there were questions about limiting his knowledge to being only -- that he only know about crimes that he was -- that were committed by his unit. That was what Mr. Lukic started out with, and I just want to clarify whether that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, his question was, Mr. Lukic's question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that the question was he only knows about conduct of his unit not crimes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Crimes is also conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- well, give us a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't go into that question, Mr. Marcussen. You cannot try by any means to give us the impression that the witness could tell us about other criminal activity, in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I withdraw it. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were asked about Ulemek or Legija. Was there anything distinguishable about him that you recognized when saw him in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a Toja [phoen] T-shirt. He was tattooed. He had some nets and a rose on his neck. He was heavily built. He had some engines on his arm, tattoos of engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You said he had a rose on his neck. Was that a tattoo or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a tattoo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You've been asked about the issue of dividing or sharing money and things that were stolen and looted, and I think we need to clarify this a little bit. You -- you said today that there were two separate incidents that you have been talking about; one in 1998 and one in 1999. Yesterday, you also spoke about two different -- you described two different things. You described sharing money that was taken from refugees, and then you described an incident where three trucks came. The sharing of the money --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- when was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the three trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's my mistake. We need a redaction, I'm afraid, to page 75, line 22, and we'll need to go -- if I can ask we go into private session for just a previous moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session. Judge Chowhan has certain questions he wishes to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: K79, you've got your wish. That brings your evidence to an end. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence and to assist the trial process. You are now free to leave the courtroom. We shall go into closed session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen is now going to surprise us by telling us which witness he's leading this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, no, I'm not. Yes. We -- we don't have any witnesses for the rest of this week, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you are going to ensure that next week is fully occupied, at least the three days we have? It's not looking too optimistic on the list I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I -- I would probably be somewhat careless if I could promise you that we would have a full list, but I do think that we will be occupying a good part of next week, at least, and I'm hopeful we will be occupying the full week. We are trying to do what we can to fill out the schedule. It really it difficult. We have several time whose entire time is taken up by this. But as we have pointed out in a filing we made, we have reached the point where it really is difficult to shuffle people around. We're doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's grateful to all who were willing to change their arrangements to accommodate the effort to complete this witness's evidence. As usual, we achieved it far more quickly than anticipated. That seems to happen regularly when we make special arrangements to extend the sitting time. That means we can now adjourn, and we shall resume on Wednesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.39 p.m.,
